nameStory: The pond fingernailclam gets its name from its tiny size and shape - it's about as small as a child's fingernail and just as thin! The "pond" part tells you where to look for these little freshwater mollusks, while "clam" indicates they're bivalves with two hinged shells like their much larger ocean cousins.
description: The pond fingernailclam is one of New England's tiniest freshwater mollusks, measuring just 3-6 millimeters long - smaller than a pea! These miniature clams have thin, translucent shells that are typically yellowish-brown to pale gray in color. Like all clams, they have two matching shell halves (called valves) connected by a flexible hinge, and they use a small muscular foot to burrow into soft sediments. You'll need to look very carefully to spot these inconspicuous little filter-feeders in ponds, streams, and wetlands.

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Extremely small at 3-6mm long - about the size of a match head or small bead, much smaller than any other clam you'll find

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Oval to slightly triangular shells that feel smooth and thin between your fingers, almost fragile like an eggshell

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Translucent yellowish-brown to pale gray shells that you can almost see through when held up to light

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy surface with very faint growth lines - feels slippery when wet and surprisingly lightweight

idTips.label: Habitat clue
idTips.description: Found buried in soft mud or sand in shallow areas, often discovered when sifting through sediment with your hands

habitat: Pond fingernailclams live in shallow freshwater environments throughout New England, including ponds, slow-moving streams, marshes, and the quiet backwater areas of rivers. They prefer soft, muddy or sandy bottoms where they can easily burrow, often in areas with aquatic plants like cattails, pondweeds, or water lilies. You'll typically find them in water less than 3 feet deep, though they can tolerate temporary drying in seasonal wetlands.

seasonality.spring: Active period begins as water warms - look for tiny tracks or disturbances in soft sediment as they move and feed near the surface.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when they're easiest to find filtering water and reproducing. Check shallow, warm areas of ponds and streams by gently sifting through the top layer of mud.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to burrow deeper into sediment. Good time to search as water levels often drop, concentrating them in smaller areas.
seasonality.winter: Buried deep in mud to survive freezing, nearly impossible to find. Wait for spring thaw to resume your search.

funFact: Despite being smaller than your thumbnail, pond fingernailclams are hermaphrodites that can actually brood their babies inside their shells - you might find a parent carrying dozens of even tinier offspring that look like specks of dust!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with juvenile Asian clams or other pea clam species, but pond fingernailclams are consistently smaller (under 6mm) and more translucent. Memory trick: if you can clearly see it without squinting, it's probably not a fingernailclam!
contextualKnowledge: The term "fingernailclam" is sometimes used loosely for any tiny freshwater clam, leading to identification confusion. True fingernailclams belong to the specific family Sphaeriidae and are much smaller than "pea clams" despite the names being used interchangeably by some sources.
compareHints: Pond fingernailclams are typically smaller and more oval-shaped than their swamp fingernailclam cousins, which tend to be slightly more triangular and prefer marshier conditions. Lake fingernailclams are usually found in deeper, clearer water and have a more consistently rounded shell shape. When in doubt, habitat is your best clue - pond species stick to shallow, weedy areas of still or slow-moving water.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Swamp fingernailclams are typically more yellowish than the pond fingernailclam and prefer muddier, more stagnant waters compared to the clearer habitats of lake fingernailclams.
Lake Fingernailclams are typically the roundest of the three Musculium species in New England, while Pond Fingernailclams tend to be more triangular and Swamp Fingernailclams are more elongated.
